claim: Did you know… stock market anomalies fade once an academic paper publishes them?

studies.finding: Published stock-return predictors earned less after publication than in their original samples, as if investors read the papers.
studies.verdict: Reported 26% lower out of sample and 58% lower after publication.

claim: Did you know… sunny mornings lift stock returns in the nearest stock exchange city?

studies.finding: Morning sunshine in each exchange city correlated with daily index returns in 26 countries from 1982 to 1997.
studies.verdict: Authors say modest trading costs erase the gains from trading on it.

studies.cite: Loughran & Schultz (2004), Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
studies.finding: Cloud cover near a firm's headquarters had little effect on its returns and created no profitable trades.
studies.verdict: Local-weather test finds almost nothing; the question stays contested.

claim: Did you know… a national team's World Cup loss drags down its stock market?

studies.cite: Edmans, García & Norli (2007), Journal of Finance
studies.finding: A country's stocks fell the next day after its national team lost, with an elimination from the World Cup near -0.5%.
studies.verdict: Original result; one later firm-level test found it disappears under panel controls.

studies.cite: Fung et al. (2015), Journal of International Financial Markets, Institutions and Money
studies.finding: Turkish firm-level data reproduced the loss effect with the original method, then lost it under panel models with spatial and time controls.
studies.verdict: Effect did not survive the stricter specification in this market.

claim: Did you know… switching to daylight saving time makes stocks slump on Monday?

studies.cite: Kamstra, Kramer & Levi (2000), American Economic Review
studies.finding: The weekend effect on Monday returns was larger after the two weekends when clocks change, attributed to lost sleep.
studies.verdict: Original claim; its size and significance were disputed.

studies.finding: A published comment disputing the daylight saving anomaly, answered by Kamstra, Kramer and Levi in the same issue.
studies.verdict: Contested from the start; the original authors replied.

studies.cite: Lamb, Zuber & Gandar (2004), Applied Financial Economics
studies.finding: A re-examination found the effect inconsistent and smaller and less significant than originally reported.
studies.verdict: Second critique; the anomaly is usually treated as unconfirmed.

claim: Did you know… sumo wrestlers throw matches for each other, and the data show it?

studies.finding: Wrestlers needing one win for a winning record won far more often than expected, and then lost the rematch.
studies.verdict: Authors found the rigging pattern vanished during periods of media scrutiny.

claim: Did you know… Olympic fighters wearing red win more often than those in blue?

studies.finding: In four Olympic combat sports in 2004, red outcompeted blue, with the edge concentrated in evenly matched bouts.
Twenty years of Olympic taekwondo showed a red edge for men under manual scoring but no overall colour effect under electronic scoring.
studies.verdict: Effect looks like referee bias that fades when judgment is automated.

claim: Did you know… lottery winners end up no happier than anyone else?

studies.cite: Brickman, Coates & Janoff-Bulman (1978), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
studies.finding: Twenty-two lottery winners rated their happiness about the same as 22 controls; accident victims scored lower.
studies.verdict: Tiny, one-time sample that became the textbook 'hedonic treadmill' example.

studies.cite: Lindqvist, Östling & Cesarini (2020), Review of Economic Studies
studies.finding: Swedish lottery winners surveyed 5 to 22 years later reported lasting gains in life satisfaction compared with matched controls.
studies.verdict: Large sample overturns the no-effect story; happiness effects were smaller.

claim: Did you know… professional hockey players are mostly born in January through March?

studies.finding: NHL, WHL and OHL players showed a steady decline in numbers from January births to December births.
studies.verdict: Original observation of the relative age effect; holds across later studies.

studies.finding: A review found birthdate skews in youth and professional leagues worldwide, in many though not all sports.
studies.verdict: Review confirms the pattern, tied to age-group cutoffs rather than talent.

claim: Did you know… referees gave visiting teams fewer yellow cards when stadiums were empty?

studies.finding: In crowdless 2019/20 football matches, away teams received fewer yellow cards, shrinking home advantage.
studies.verdict: Natural experiment from the pandemic; effect on cards was large.

studies.cite: Leitner et al. (2023), Management Review Quarterly
studies.finding: A review of ghost-game studies found home advantage fell, attributed mainly to less referee bias and less fan support.
studies.verdict: No reviewed study found home advantage rising.

claim: Did you know… NFL teams overpay for high draft picks, and have for decades?

studies.finding: Early draft picks were priced well above the surplus value their players actually delivered, despite experienced decision makers.
studies.verdict: Archival result; no later study located here that overturns it.
